h1:
Koh Samui Viewpoints
Lad Koh, Chaweng Noi + Sea Photo Spots Around the Island
intro: Part of Koh Samui's charm is that a single loop around the island takes barely an hour, yet you pass plenty of ocean viewpoints along the way — from Lad Koh (Hin Lat), where you can park right beside the road and walk down to the sea, to the clifftop cafes above Chaweng Noi where people gather for sunset. We've rounded up the spots that are genuinely open and reachable right now, and we'll tell you straight which ones are free, which charge a fee, and which angle photographs best at which time of day.

blocks.html: If you've rented a scooter or car on Samui, viewpoints are what make looping the island so much more fun — because the ring road (Highway 4169) hugs the east coast for long stretches, and every time you crest a rise you get a curving bay below you with little islands floating out on the horizon. We've ordered these from the easiest to reach (just pull over on the roadside) to the ones where you have to drive up a hill or hike up yourself.

blocks.text: Lad Koh Viewpoint (Hin Lat) — the star spot on the ring road

blocks.html: Lad Koh Viewpoint, which most people simply call Hin Lat, sits right on the 4169 ring road between Chaweng Noi and Lamai beaches — about 10–15 minutes' drive from Chaweng. It's known for its panoramic view of the east coast: a curving bay, blue-green water, and small islands scattered across the sea. There's a Thai-roofed pavilion where you can sit and listen to the waves, plus a concrete path leading down to the rocks at the water's edge.

items: Entry: Free, open all day, no one collecting money.
Parking: A small roadside lot — fine for a scooter or car.
What's for sale: Ice cream, drinking water, coffee, and a few small photo spots up top.
Best time: Early morning for soft light, or late afternoon when the sun isn't harsh — there's no shade from trees down below.

blocks.title: A safety warning
blocks.html: Don't go swimming at Hin Lat — the waves are strong, there's no sandy beach, just bare rocks. If you climb onto the rocks for photos, watch your footing when the waves wash over them, and don't clamber out to the very edge for a shot.

blocks.text: Chaweng Noi and the east coast — the clifftop spots with the widest views

blocks.html: Up the hill from Hin Lat above Chaweng Noi is the zone with the most open view on the island — you can see Chaweng Bay, Chaweng Noi Bay, and the Gulf of Thailand all at once. The cafes and restaurants on this hillside have become the popular sunset gathering spots.

items.name: Jungle Club
items.blurb: Perched on the Chaweng Noi hillside with a deck that juts out from the cliff face. Sink into a beanbag with a drink and take in the Gulf of Thailand and the Chaweng coastline. It gets busy in the evening, so book a table ahead if you're coming for a sunset dinner. The access road is very steep — if you're not confident on a scooter, take the venue's shuttle.

items.name: Coral Cove
items.blurb: On the road between Chaweng Noi and Lamai there's a steep rise at Coral Cove with a pretty view of the sea and rocks, plus several seaview restaurants worth stopping at. A good spot to pull over for a photo on the way.

blocks.text: Lamai Viewpoint + Hin Ta Hin Yai — views paired with oddly shaped rocks

blocks.html: The southern side around Lamai has viewpoints paired with strangely shaped boulders, which are the photo highlight of this zone.

items: Lamai Viewpoint + Valentine Stone: There's a small cafe selling coffee and drinks at the viewpoint. Entry is about 50 THB per person if you walk up yourself, or around 100 THB for the tram up and down. There's a small waterfall in the same area too.

Hin Ta Hin Yai (Grandfather and Grandmother Rocks): The comically shaped seaside rocks that are Lamai's landmark. A short walk from the parking lot, free to enter, with a market of snacks and souvenirs all around.

Overlap Stone: Two giant boulders resting on top of each other on the hill. A short steep climb gets you up, where you'll see the view of the island's southern coastline — good for anyone who likes an unusual angle.

blocks.title: Straight talk on entry fees
blocks.html: Several of the clifftop viewpoints on the Lamai side are privately run and charge 20–100 THB for entry or parking depending on the spot, with prices that can shift by season. If you'd rather not pay, Hin Lat and Hin Ta Hin Yai are free, while Valentine Stone and Overlap Stone charge. Check the price sign at the entrance before you decide.

items.name: Khao Hua Jook Chedi
items.blurb: A golden chedi on a hill near the airport — you can spot it as your plane comes in to land. Drive up to the top for an almost 360-degree view around the island, including the airport and Bophut Bay. Free to enter and not crowded, so it's a good quiet stop in the late afternoon.

items.name: Wat Phra Yai (Big Buddha)
items.blurb: A large golden Buddha image on a small island off the north coast — Samui's landmark photo spot. The view looks out over the northern sea and the boats running to Koh Phangan. Climb the steps to pay respects, then take in the view.

blocks.html: If you really want the sun setting over the sea, you'll need the west coast around Nathon or the island's western beaches — because on the east coast (Chaweng–Lamai) the sun rises out of the sea, which makes it better for sunrise than sunset.

blocks.text: When the photos turn out best

items: Sunrise (around 6am): Hin Lat, Chaweng Noi, and the east coast — soft light, clear water, few people.
Sunset (5pm–6:30pm): Jungle Club, Khao Hua Jook, and the west coast at Nathon.
Harsh midday sun: Avoid the clifftop spots with no shade. The water looks gorgeous but the sun is hot and you'll be shooting into the light — bring a hat and water.

blocks.text: What to watch out for driving around the island

blocks.html: Many of Samui's viewpoints sit on steep hills, especially the climbs up to Jungle Club, Coral Cove, and Khao Hua Jook. If you're on a scooter, you need to be confident in your bike and your own braking.

items: Some hill climbs are steep and narrow — new riders shouldn't push it. The venue shuttle or a hired car is safer.
Wear a helmet every time. Police set up checkpoints often on the island, and the roads get slick and slippery in the rainy season.
Check the forecast before you head out. During the monsoon (roughly Oct–Dec), rain comes down hard, the sea gets rough, and the view can be socked in by cloud.
Fuel is hard to find on the hill roads — fill up before you head uphill.

faq.q: Is Lad Koh Viewpoint (Hin Lat) free to enter?
faq.a: Yes, it's free with no one collecting an entry fee. It sits on the 4169 ring road between Chaweng Noi and Lamai, with a small roadside parking lot. Park, walk down to the sea, and take your photos — but don't go swimming, as the waves are strong and it's all rocks.

faq.q: Which Koh Samui viewpoint is good for watching the sunset?
faq.a: If you want the sun actually setting over the sea, you'll need the west coast around Nathon. On the hills, spots like Jungle Club and Khao Hua Jook still catch lovely evening light. East-coast spots like Hin Lat and Chaweng Noi are better suited to sunrise.

faq.q: Do I need to book ahead for Jungle Club?
faq.a: It gets busy at sunset, so book a table in advance. The access road is also very steep — if you're not used to riding a scooter, take the venue's shuttle to be safe.

faq.q: How much do Koh Samui viewpoints charge to enter?
faq.a: Several are free, including Hin Lat, Hin Ta Hin Yai, and Khao Hua Jook. Privately run spots like Lamai Viewpoint / Valentine Stone charge around 50 THB if you walk up yourself, or 100 THB for the tram. Some charge 20 THB for parking. Prices can change, so check the sign at the entrance.

faq.q: Is riding a scooter to the clifftop viewpoints dangerous?
faq.a: Several hill climbs are steep and narrow, especially Jungle Club, Coral Cove, and Khao Hua Jook. New riders should take care or use a shuttle, wear a helmet every time, and avoid riding in the rain since the roads get slippery.
